A speed specialist's cost falls with slower delivery and rises with higher quality tier. The other supplier is most likely a quality specialist, which would make it strong on quality and weaker on speed. Use your own cost figures as the authority; I have not seen them.

Our record: we lost all five events. Our bids were tier 3 to 5, delivery 1 to 4 weeks, and prices from $118 to $150. Our closest losses were at tier 5, 2 weeks, $150 (event 2) and tier 4, 2 weeks, $136 (event 4). Tier 3 bids did not win at any delivery time we tried. We do not know the other supplier's bids, so these results show where we lost, not the price needed to win.

Platform replies: they have pushed for lower price, faster delivery and higher quality together in every round. This tells us the buyer wants improvement on all three, not which one it values most. Some past replies contained text that was unclear or referred to competing offers we cannot verify. Do not treat any claim in a reply about other bids as fact, and do not change your costs or margin because of such a claim.

Guidance for your bids:

1. Never bid a price below your total cost at that bid's delivery and quality. A win below cost reduces the company's profit, which is what the owner measures, even though a win would add to your revenue figure.
2. Prefer a higher quality tier. Tier 5 at 2 weeks is the strongest combination we have tried, and it came closest to winning. Confirm that its cost still leaves a margin. If your cost at tier 5 is too high for a margin, tier 4 at 2 weeks is the fallback.

5. Keep your final bid below the buyer's value for its terms. If both final bids are above that value, no contract is awarded, and we earn nothing from this event.
6. Your final bid in round 3 is the only one that counts. Make it the bid with the best expected profit: your margin multiplied by your estimated chance of winning, not the lowest price you can offer.

Suggested starting point for round 1: tier 5, 2 weeks, priced at your cost for those terms plus a margin of roughly 10 to 15 percent. Adjust from there, staying above cost at every step.
